Distribution. Korea (Gyeonggi-do, new record), China (Liaoning), Japan (Hokkaido, Honshu, Kyushu, Shikoku), Siberia (Far East). Stream information. Two streams, the only localities where larvae and pupae of S. konoi were collected so far, were separated by Mt. Myeongjisan (1,267 m) by a distance of 4.6 km. Both streams were medium to large-sized streams with moderate to rapid flow and stream beds consisting of boulders and rubble, and totally exposed to the sun. Edges of the streams were lined with trailing vegetations including reeds. The streams were 10 - 20 m wide and 15 - 20 cm deep, but the streams were partially dried up due to spring drought. Biological notes. Larvae were collected from trailing vegetation, submerged twigs, and dead leaves. Body colors of fresh larvae were brownish red or brownish grey when fully matured. Specimens were collected along with Prosimulium kiotoense, Simulium japonicum, Simulium malyschevi, Simulium suzukii, and Simulium yamatoense (the latter was previously misidentified as S. rufibasis). All larvae and pupae were collected only twice in May 2019 from two streams, and I failed to collect S. konoi in subsequent attempts in other months at the same streams, suggesting S. konoi is univoltine as Sato et al. (2004) suggested. In Japan as well, larvae and pupae of S. konoi were collected only in April and had not been found in other months (Sato et al., 2004).

Distribution. Central Nepal, China (South Tibet). Note. The genus and species were revised, re-described and illustrated by Behounek et al. (2013). Formerly the species has been known from two localities in Central Nepal only. The new record of P. yangzisherpana in South Tibet (China) significantly extends the range of its known distribution. As in the Nepal populations, the species occurs in Tibet in upper part of Picea-Betula forest belt at altitude of 3250 m.
